what_it_does: Processing-in-memory (PIM) — doing arithmetic directly inside the memory chip rather than sending data to a separate processor — is a promising way to run AI workloads faster because it avoids the bottleneck of shuttling data back and forth. DRAM memory is organized into banks (independent sub-arrays that can each do one operation at a time), and running many banks in parallel is important for speed. The problem addressed here is that when all banks must stay in lockstep (synchronized), the time spent waking up each bank's memory rows (called row activation) takes longer than the actual computation, wasting most of the time. Letting banks run independently (asynchronously) hides that wasted time, but then each bank needs its own accumulator circuit to collect partial results, which takes a lot of chip area. This paper proposes a middle path: group the banks into clusters called bank groups, let different groups run independently of each other (to hide row-activation delays), but keep banks within the same group synchronized with each other (so they can share one accumulator per group rather than one per bank). This hybrid reduces both idle time and chip area.
